transcript.text:
High in the Shiverbacks, where the wind off the snowfields smells of iron and cold stone, lies Greyhollow: a mining town cut into the mountain's flank, its streets little more than ledges and its heartbeat the ringing of the smithies. Brakka Ironvein has served six years as a guard at the Temple of the Anvil Father, and the town has become as familiar to him as the heft of his own hammer.

But not the old north workings. Those were sealed a generation ago, and the warning softened over time into silence. Three days ago three miners went down. None came back. Last night a fourth man came up alone, raving about lights that walk, and died before dawn. At sunrise the town council will brick the entrance shut, missing or not. Prior Hessa, old and grey as the mountain, has asked Brakka to go down before then and bring back whoever can still be brought back.

Now it is late afternoon. Brakka stands at the mine mouth, a mile north of Greyhollow's last houses, the unlit temple lantern heavy in his hand. The opening is a low black arch shored with grey timbers, and the boards that once sealed it stand prized loose around the threshold. Cold air moves out of it, smelling of wet stone and, faintly, of smoke. The day's last light lies thin on the slope behind him. He has until sunrise.

What do you do?

I light the temple lantern and check the threshold first, looking for fresh boot prints, drag marks, or anything the miners left behind in the dirt. Then I step into the arch with my hammer ready, keeping to the middle of the tunnel and watching the shoring timbers as I go.

Brakka Ironvein has served six years as a guard at the Temple of the Anvil Father, and the town has become as familiar to him as the heft of his own hammer.

But not the old north workings. Those were sealed a generation ago, and the warning softened over time into silence. Three days ago three miners went down. None came back. Last night a fourth man came up alone, raving about lights that walk, and died before dawn. At sunrise the town council will brick the entrance shut, missing or not. Prior Hessa, old and grey as the mountain, has asked Brakka to go down before then and bring back whoever can still be brought back.

Now it is late afternoon. Brakka stands at the mine mouth, a mile north of Greyhollow's last houses, the unlit temple lantern heavy in his hand. The opening is a low black arch shored with grey timbers, and the boards that once sealed it stand prized loose around the threshold. Cold air moves out of it, smelling of wet stone and, faintly, of smoke. The day's last light lies thin on the slope behind him. He has until sunrise.

What do you do?
